content: The sensitivity of rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) for syphilis ranges from 85% to 98%, while their specificity ranges from 93% to 98%, when compared to reference standards such as the Treponema pallidum hemagglutination assay (TPHA) or the Treponema pallidum particle agglutination assay (TPPA). Generally, RDTs with higher sensitivity tend to have lower specificity, and vice versa. Most of the initial RDTs utilize Treponema pallidum antigens to detect treponema-specific antibodies. Many of these tests employ immunochromatographic strips, which are impregnated with treponemal antigens that react with syphilis antibodies present in whole blood or serum. More recently, tests capable of detecting antibodies against cardiolipin-like materials have been developed. These tests operate on principles similar to other non-treponemal tests and are available in combination with treponemal RDTs. This dual approach provides both a screening component (equivalent to RPR/VDRL) and a confirmatory component (equivalent to TPHA/TPPA). However, these dual RDTs have not yet undergone sufficient evaluation or field testing to be recommended for widespread use. The guidelines for syphilis treatment require review and reassessment, particularly in light of recent evidence regarding the effectiveness and antimicrobial susceptibility patterns of azithromycin. Benzathine penicillin has been the standard treatment for syphilis for over 70 years. Doxycycline is recommended as an alternative treatment for non-pregnant patients allergic to penicillin. Some studies suggest that azithromycin may be as effective as benzathine penicillin for treating early syphilis. Azithromycin offers the advantage of single-dose oral administration and should be considered as a potential alternative for penicillin-allergic pregnant patients. However, this advantage must be weighed against the increasing reports of Treponema pallidum resistance to azithromycin. Other options for treating penicillin-allergic patients, such as desensitization and daily injectable ceftriaxone, should also be explored. The 2003 WHO guidelines for managing sexually transmitted infections (STIs) recommend early screening and treatment of pregnant women with syphilis, ideally before the second trimester, to prevent fetal complications. These guidelines also include recommendations for treating early and late congenital syphilis. Based on these recommendations, healthcare providers must diagnose and differentiate between early and late congenital syphilis. Diagnosing congenital syphilis remains challenging, as it requires clinical expertise and access to laboratory tests. These guidelines are intended for healthcare providers at all levels of the healthcare system—primary, secondary, and tertiary—who are involved in the treatment and management of STIs in low-, middle-, and high-income countries. They are also aimed at individuals working in sexual and reproductive health programs, such as those addressing HIV/AIDS, family planning, maternal and child health, and adolescent health, to ensure appropriate STI diagnosis and management. The guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations for treating specific clinical conditions caused by Treponema pallidum. They serve as a framework for countries to develop national treatment recommendations, taking into account local antimicrobial resistance patterns, healthcare service capacity, and available resources. Updated treatment recommendations based on the latest evidence are included for the most common conditions caused by Treponema pallidum, such as early latent syphilis, late latent syphilis, and congenital syphilis. Recommendations for rare conditions, including neurosyphilis and tertiary syphilis (e.g., gummatous and cardiovascular syphilis), were not updated due to a lack of new information since the 2003 WHO STI guidelines. To update the WHO guidelines for the prevention, treatment, and management of STIs, a Guideline Development Group (GDG) was established, comprising 33 international STI experts, including clinicians, researchers, and program managers. A core subgroup focused specifically on syphilis-related guidelines to provide intensive feedback throughout the process. The GDG participated in meetings and teleconferences to prioritize questions, discuss evidence reviews, and finalize recommendations. Systematic reviews for each priority question were conducted by McMaster University, a WHO Collaborating Centre for Evidence-Informed Policy. Evidence was reviewed for desirable and undesirable outcomes, patient values and preferences, resource use, acceptability, equity, and feasibility. The quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach, which categorizes evidence into four levels: high, moderate, low, and very low. The direct costs of medicines were estimated using the 2014 edition of the Management Sciences for Health (MSH) International Drug Price Indicator Guide. Recommendations were developed during a second GDG meeting in October 2015, facilitated by co-chairs with expertise in GRADE and clinical STI management. The GDG reached consensus on all recommendations without the need for voting. The finalized recommendations were peer-reviewed and approved by an External Review Group. The strength of each recommendation was rated as either strong or conditional. Strong recommendations are phrased as The WHO STI guideline recommends…, while conditional recommendations are phrased as The WHO STI guideline suggests…. The implications of these differing strengths for patients, clinicians, and policymakers are explained in detail within the guidelines. Conflict of interest management was a key priority throughout the guideline development process. Declaration of Interest (DOI) statements were obtained from all GDG members, and no significant conflicts of interest were identified that would exclude any member from fully participating in the process. The guidelines will be disseminated as a printed publication, a downloadable document on the WHO website, and through the WHO Reproductive Health Library. They will also be available in a guideline application created with GRADEpro GDT software. WHO headquarters will collaborate with regional and country offices to support the adaptation, implementation, and monitoring of these guidelines. Partnerships with organizations such as UNFPA, UNICEF, UNAIDS, and NGOs will ensure integration into sexual and reproductive health services. A system for monitoring new evidence and updating recommendations will be established within a year of guideline implementation. An electronic follow-up survey of key end-users will identify challenges, barriers, and gaps in treatment to inform future editions. Countries are encouraged to conduct high-quality studies to adapt the guidelines to their local STI epidemiology and antimicrobial resistance patterns. In areas lacking local data, the recommendations can be adopted as presented.
